title: 77 Labour MPs Demand Starmer Quit After Historic Rout
excerpt: A make-or-break speech on Monday failed to stop a mounting rebellion inside Labour after the party's worst local election result in decades.
body:
Seventy-seven Labour MPs are now openly calling for Prime Minister Keir Starmer to resign or set a departure timetable — and the number keeps climbing. The revolt erupted after May 7 local elections delivered a crushing verdict on his government, and a high-profile Monday address designed to steady the ship instead accelerated the mutiny.

What happened at the ballot box: Labour lost 1,496 councillors and lost control of 38 councils, a historic collapse. Speculation about the prime minister's future intensified since the elections, in which Labour lost almost 1,500 English councillors, went backwards in Scotland and slumped to third in Wales. Right-wing populist Reform UK, led by Nigel Farage — a Trump ally and central figure in the Brexit movement — made significant gains.

Why Starmer's speech made things worse: Four government aides resigned, joining dozens of Labour MPs calling for Starmer to stand down, within hours of the prime minister making a speech promising sweeping changes designed to unite the party. Keir Starmer insisted he would 'not walk away' as Prime Minister and that after the election results 'the right thing to do is rebuild and show the path forward.' But several allies of Health Secretary Wes Streeting were among those calling on Starmer to go, fuelling speculation that Streeting could soon launch a challenge against the prime minister. Potential challengers to the leadership include Health Secretary Wes Streeting, former Deputy Prime Minister Angela Rayner and Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham.

What to watch next: A leadership challenge requires the endorsement of 81 Labour MPs — a threshold that, with 77 names already public, could fall within days, making this week the most consequential in Starmer's premiership.

nri_angle: With over 1.5 million British Indians holding close ties to the UK — and Labour's traditional alignment with South Asian diaspora communities — a Labour leadership change could reshape immigration, trade, and foreign-policy stances that directly affect Indian-Americans with family and business interests in Britain.
